name: Bhutan
summary: A white thunder dragon (Druk) lies along the diagonal dividing a yellow upper-hoist half from an orange lower-fly half. The dragon gives the country its own name, Druk Yul, 'Land of the Thunder Dragon'.
origin: Bhutan's first flag was designed in 1949 for the signing of a treaty with India; it was square and divided yellow and red with a green dragon. Later in the 1950s and 1960s the dragon became white and the lower colour shifted to orange.

The modern form was standardised around 1969, and in 1972 the National Assembly codified the flag's design and the meaning of each element. The 2008 Constitution describes the flag in its first schedule.

colors.name: Yellow
colors.meaning: The secular authority and tradition of the Druk Gyalpo, the Dragon King.

colors.name: Orange
colors.meaning: Buddhist spiritual practice, especially the Drukpa Kagyu and Nyingma traditions.

colors.name: White
colors.meaning: Purity and the loyalty of Bhutan's diverse peoples.

symbols.name: Druk (Thunder Dragon)
symbols.description: A white dragon facing away from the hoist, lying centred along the dividing line between the two halves.
symbols.meaning: The name of the country and of the Drukpa school of Buddhism; its placement over both halves shows the equal importance of secular and religious authority.

symbols.name: Norbu (jewels)
symbols.description: Jewels clutched in the dragon's claws.
symbols.meaning: The wealth and prosperity of the country and the security of its people.

symbols.name: Snarling mouth
symbols.description: The dragon's open, snarling jaws.
symbols.meaning: The strength of the deities protecting Bhutan.

history.label: First flag
history.note: Nearly square, yellow and red with a green dragon.

history.label: Transitional versions
history.note: White dragon; the lower half moved from red toward orange.

history.label: Current flag
history.note: Codified by the National Assembly in 1972.

facts: The dragon must be white, never green or any other colour.
It is one of a few national flags featuring a dragon; Wales's flag also has one, but Wales is a constituent country, not a sovereign state.
Bhutanese call their country Druk Yul, 'Land of the Thunder Dragon'.
clues: A white dragon lies across a diagonal split of yellow and orange.
Its emblem clutches jewels in its claws.
One half represents royal authority and the other a Buddhist tradition.
The creature on it is also part of the country's name in its own language.

name: Brazil
designer: Raimundo Teixeira Mendes and Miguel Lemos, with Manuel Pereira Reis (astronomy) and Décio Villares (artwork)
summary: A yellow rhombus on a green field, holding a blue celestial globe that shows the sky over Rio de Janeiro on the morning the Republic was proclaimed. A white band across it carries the positivist motto 'Ordem e Progresso'.
origin: The green field and yellow rhombus come from the imperial flag of 1822. Green was the colour of the House of Braganza of Emperor Pedro I, and yellow that of the House of Habsburg-Lorraine of his wife, Empress Maria Leopoldina.

After the monarchy fell on 15 November 1889, the Republic briefly used a flag modelled on the US Stars and Stripes. Four days later, on 19 November, Decree No. 4 adopted the present design, which kept the imperial colours and replaced the imperial arms with a globe of stars.
The designers were followers of Auguste Comte's positivism, and the motto shortens Comte's formula: 'Love as a principle and order as the basis; progress as the goal.'

colors.name: Green
colors.meaning: Originally the House of Braganza; popularly read as Brazil's forests.

colors.name: Yellow
colors.meaning: Originally the House of Habsburg-Lorraine; popularly read as Brazil's gold and mineral wealth.

colors.name: Blue
colors.meaning: The night sky over Rio de Janeiro.

colors.name: White
colors.meaning: The band carrying the motto, and the stars.

symbols.name: Celestial globe with 27 stars
symbols.description: Nine constellations, including the Southern Cross, Scorpius and Canis Major, shown as they appeared from Rio de Janeiro at about 8:30 a.m. on 15 November 1889, as if seen from outside the celestial sphere.
symbols.meaning: Each star represents one federal unit: the 26 states and the Federal District. Sirius stands for Mato Grosso; the lone star above the band, Spica, stands for Pará.

symbols.name: Motto band
symbols.description: A curved white band reading 'ORDEM E PROGRESSO' in green capitals.
symbols.meaning: 'Order and Progress', from Auguste Comte's positivist philosophy.

symbols.name: Rhombus
symbols.description: A yellow diamond inset from the edges of the green field.
symbols.meaning: Inherited from the 1822 imperial flag, where the lozenge shape was reportedly influenced by French military colours.

history.note: Green and yellow stripes with a blue canton of stars, used for four days.

history.label: 21 stars
history.note: The original republican design.

history.label: 22 stars
history.note: A star added for the state of Guanabara.

history.label: 23 stars
history.note: Stars rearranged and added for new states.

history.label: 27 stars
history.note: Law 8.421 of 1992 added stars for Amapá, Roraima, Rondônia and Tocantins.

facts: Brazil is one of very few national flags to show a real moment in the sky.
Law 5.700 of 1971 governs the flag; stars must be added or removed if states are created or abolished.
The sky is mirrored relative to what an observer on the ground would see, a point argued over since 1889.
clues: A yellow diamond on green, with a starry blue globe crossed by a white motto band.
Its stars show a real night sky from the morning a monarchy fell.
Its motto comes from a French philosopher's school of thought.
Its green and yellow came from the dynasties of an emperor and his Austrian wife.

name: Canada
designer: George F. G. Stanley (concept); leaf stylised by Jacques Saint-Cyr
summary: A red field with a white square in the centre bearing a stylised eleven-pointed red maple leaf. It replaced the Canadian Red Ensign after the 'Great Flag Debate' of 1964.
origin: Before 1965 Canada used the Union Flag and, unofficially but widely, the Canadian Red Ensign: a red British ensign with the Canadian coat of arms in the fly. The maple leaf had been a Canadian emblem since the 19th century and appeared on regimental badges and war graves.

Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson pushed for a distinctive flag before the 1967 centennial. His preferred 'Pearson Pennant' had three red leaves between blue bars, which led to months of debate in Parliament in 1964. A 15-member parliamentary committee received thousands of submissions and chose a design based on a proposal by historian George Stanley, inspired by the flag of the Royal Military College of Canada.
The House of Commons approved it on 15 December 1964, Queen Elizabeth II proclaimed it on 28 January 1965, and it was first raised on 15 February 1965, now marked as National Flag of Canada Day.

colors.name: Red
colors.meaning: One of Canada's two official colours, proclaimed by King George V in 1921; red recalls the St George's Cross and the sacrifice of Canadians in the First World War.

colors.name: White
colors.meaning: The other official colour, linked to the royal arms of France.

symbols.name: Maple leaf
symbols.description: A single stylised red sugar maple leaf with eleven points, centred on a white square (the 'Canadian pale') that is as wide as the flag is tall.
symbols.meaning: Canada and its people. The number of points has no meaning; it was chosen because a leaf with more points blurred when tested in a wind tunnel.

symbols.name: Red bars
symbols.description: Red panels at hoist and fly, each one quarter of the flag's length.
symbols.meaning: Often said to evoke the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, though this is not an official meaning.

history.label: Canadian Red Ensign (early versions)
history.note: Red ensign with a shield of the provincial arms, used unofficially.

history.label: Canadian Red Ensign with the 1921 arms
Canadian Red Ensign with green leaves
history.note: The arms' maple leaves were changed from green to red in 1957.

facts: The central white square is called a 'Canadian pale' in heraldry, after this flag.
Peru's flag has a similar red-white-red vertical layout but with equal bands.
The Royal Union Flag remains an official flag of Canada, flown alongside the national flag on certain days.
clues: Red bars on either side of a white square containing a single red leaf.
Its leaf has eleven points, chosen after wind-tunnel testing.
A heraldic term for a central square as wide as the flag is tall is named after it.
It replaced a red ensign after a long parliamentary debate in 1964.

name: Denmark
description: transcontinental sovereign state and constitutional monarchy
summary: A white Nordic cross on red, its vertical arm shifted toward the hoist. Usually described as the oldest national flag in continuous use, it is the model for every other Nordic cross flag.
origin: According to legend, the flag fell from the sky during the Battle of Lyndanisse in Estonia on 15 June 1219, turning the battle for King Valdemar II. The story first appears in writings of the early 16th century, about three hundred years after the event.

By the 14th century a red banner with a white cross was associated with the Danish kings: the Gelre Armorial (c. 1370–1386) shows a banner of this design beside the Danish royal arms. A red banner with a white cross was used as a war flag in the 15th and 16th centuries.

By the 17th century the Dannebrog was also flown by Danish merchant ships, and 1625 is commonly given as the date it was standardised as a national flag. A 1748 ordinance fixed the proportions of the merchant flag's cross, 3:1:3 vertically and 3:1:4.5 horizontally, still used today.

colors.name: Red
colors.meaning: No official meaning; red war banners with a white cross were associated with the crusades and the Holy Roman Empire.

colors.name: White
colors.meaning: The Christian cross.

symbols.name: Nordic cross
symbols.description: A white cross whose vertical arm is set toward the hoist, so the fly arms are longer.
symbols.meaning: Christianity; the off-centre arm makes the cross look centred when the flag flies.

history.label: Royal and war banner
history.note: Red with a white cross, documented from the 14th century.

history.label: Dannebrog
history.note: Used continuously as a national and merchant flag.

facts: Valdemarsdag, 15 June, commemorates the legendary fall of the flag from the sky.
The state and naval flag is a swallowtail (Splitflag) in a darker red.
The flags of Sweden, Norway, Finland, Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Åland all follow its cross design.
clues: A white off-centre cross on a red field.
Legend says it fell from the sky during a battle in 1219.
Every other flag of its regional cross family is modelled on it.
Often called the oldest national flag still in continuous use.

summary: A vertical tricolour of blue, white and red. Born in the French Revolution, it became one of the most imitated flag designs in the world and the model for revolutionary and republican tricolours across Europe and Latin America.
origin: Blue and red were the traditional colours of Paris. In July 1789, days after the storming of the Bastille, the Paris militia adopted a blue-and-red cockade; the Marquis de Lafayette is credited with adding white, the colour of the Bourbon monarchy, to symbolise the union of the king and the people of Paris.

The cockade's colours moved onto flags in the early 1790s, first in the navy. On 15 February 1794 (27 Pluviôse Year II) the National Convention decreed the vertical blue-white-red tricolour as the national flag, reportedly following a design by the painter Jacques-Louis David, with blue at the hoist.

After Napoleon's fall the restored Bourbons replaced it with the plain white royal flag (1815–1830). The July Revolution of 1830 brought the tricolour back for good. In 1848 Alphonse de Lamartine famously resisted calls to replace it with the red flag of the revolutionaries. Article 2 of the 1958 Constitution names the tricolour, blue, white and red, as the national emblem.

colors.name: Blue
colors.meaning: One of the two historic colours of the city of Paris; also linked to Saint Martin.

colors.name: White
colors.meaning: The colour of the Bourbon monarchy, added to the Paris colours in 1789 to signify king and people united.

colors.name: Red
colors.meaning: The other historic colour of Paris; also linked to Saint Denis and the Oriflamme banner.

history.label: Royal and naval flags of the Kingdom of France
history.note: Plain white or white with fleurs-de-lis served as the royal and naval colours; there was no single national flag.

history.label: Early naval tricolour
history.note: A white naval ensign with a small tricolour canton was used from 1790.

history.label: Tricolour of the Republic and Empire
history.note: Decreed on 15 February 1794 and kept by Napoleon.

history.label: Bourbon Restoration white flag
history.note: The tricolour was banned; the royal white flag returned.

history.label: Tricolour restored
history.note: Reinstated by Louis-Philippe after the July Revolution. From the mid-1970s a lighter blue was used, and in 2020 the darker navy blue was brought back into use at the Élysée.

facts: Its blue, white and red vertical design inspired dozens of later tricolours, including those of Italy, Ireland, Belgium, Romania and Mexico.
In the mid-1970s, under President Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, a lighter blue was introduced, reportedly to match the European flag; in 2020 the Élysée quietly returned to the darker navy shade.
The French Navy uses unequal stripe widths (30:33:37) so the flag appears equal when it flies at sea.
clues: A vertical tricolour with blue at the hoist and red at the fly.
The colours of its capital city were combined with the white of a royal dynasty during a revolution.
Its navy flies a version with unequal stripes so it looks even in the wind.
Decreed by a revolutionary assembly in 1794, it was banned for fifteen years after an emperor's fall.

name: Germany
summary: A horizontal tricolour of black, red and gold. The colours come from the liberal and nationalist movements of the 19th century and stand for German unity, democracy and freedom, in contrast with the black-white-red of the German Empire.
origin: During the Napoleonic Wars the volunteer Lützow Free Corps wore black uniforms with red facings and gold (brass) buttons. Its veterans helped found the student fraternities (Burschenschaften), whose black-red-gold banners appeared at the Wartburg Festival of 1817 and the Hambach Festival of 1832, the first great democratic rally in Germany.

The colours were also believed, inaccurately, to be those of the medieval Holy Roman Empire (a black eagle with red claws on gold). In 1848 the Frankfurt Parliament adopted black-red-gold as the flag of a hoped-for united, liberal Germany, but the revolution failed.

Bismarck's North German Confederation and the German Empire used black-white-red instead. The Weimar Republic restored black-red-gold in 1919; the Nazis abolished it in 1933. In 1949 both German states chose black-red-gold. West Germany's Basic Law (Article 22) defined the federal flag; East Germany added its hammer-and-compass emblem in 1959. Reunification in 1990 brought the plain tricolour to all of Germany.

colors.name: Black
colors.meaning: From the Lützow Free Corps uniforms; often explained as the darkness of oppression overcome.

colors.name: Red
colors.meaning: From the Lützow uniform facings; often explained as blood shed for freedom.

colors.name: Gold
colors.meaning: From the brass buttons; often explained as the golden light of freedom. Officially gold, not yellow.

history.label: German Confederation (Frankfurt Parliament)
history.note: Black-red-gold as the flag of the 1848 revolution.

history.label: North German Confederation and German Empire
history.note: Black-white-red, combining Prussian black and white with Hanseatic red and white.

history.label: Weimar Republic
history.note: Black-red-gold restored; the merchant flag kept black-white-red with a black-red-gold canton.

history.label: Nazi Germany
history.note: Black-white-red until 1935, then the swastika flag as sole national flag.

history.label: Federal Republic of Germany
history.note: Black-red-gold, defined in Article 22 of the Basic Law; extended to reunified Germany in 1990.

history.label: German Democratic Republic
history.note: Black-red-gold with the hammer, compass and ring of rye.

facts: Federal government offices fly a version with the federal shield (the Bundesdienstflagge), which private citizens may not use.
Belgium has the same colours in vertical bands and a nearly square ratio.
Displaying Nazi flags is a criminal offence in Germany; the Imperial black-white-red flag is legal but is restricted in some states because extremists use it.
clues: Three horizontal bands: black on top, then red, then gold.
Its colours trace back to the uniforms of a volunteer corps that fought Napoleon.
A revolutionary parliament adopted it in 1848, but it became official only in 1919.
For forty years two neighbouring states used it, one with a hammer and compass added.

name: India
designer: Based on a design by Pingali Venkayya
summary: A horizontal tricolour of saffron, white and green with a navy-blue 24-spoke wheel, the Ashoka Chakra, at its centre. It was adopted by the Constituent Assembly three weeks before independence.
origin: Several flags were used during the independence movement, including the Calcutta flag of 1906 and Bhikaiji Cama's flag raised in Stuttgart in 1907. In 1921 Pingali Venkayya presented Mahatma Gandhi with a red and green design for the Indian National Congress; at Gandhi's suggestion a white stripe and a spinning wheel (charkha) were added.
In 1931 the Congress adopted the Swaraj flag: saffron, white and green with a blue charkha in the centre. To avoid communal readings it declared that the colours had no religious meaning.

On 22 July 1947 the Constituent Assembly adopted the flag with one change: the charkha was replaced by the Dharma Chakra from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath. The wheel has no back or front, so it looks the same on both sides of the flag.

colors.name: India saffron
colors.meaning: Courage and sacrifice; in S. Radhakrishnan's explanation to the Constituent Assembly, renunciation and disinterestedness.

colors.name: White
colors.meaning: Truth, peace and light, the path of truth to guide conduct.

colors.name: India green
colors.meaning: Faith, fertility and the relation to the soil and plant life on which all life depends.

colors.name: Navy blue
colors.meaning: The colour of the Ashoka Chakra.

symbols.name: Ashoka Chakra
symbols.description: A navy-blue wheel with 24 spokes, its diameter roughly equal to the width of the white band.
symbols.meaning: The wheel of dharma (law and righteousness) from the 3rd-century BCE Lion Capital of Emperor Ashoka; Radhakrishnan described it as the wheel of motion, meaning there is life in movement and death in stagnation.

history.label: Early independence-movement flags
history.note: Including the Calcutta flag and the flag raised by Bhikaiji Cama in 1907.

history.label: Gandhi's flag
history.note: White, green and red stripes with a charkha.

history.label: Swaraj flag
history.note: Saffron, white and green with a blue charkha; the Indian National Congress flag.

history.label: National flag
history.note: Adopted 22 July 1947 with the Ashoka Chakra.

facts: The Flag Code of India long required the national flag to be made of hand-spun khadi; amendments in 2021 and 2022 permitted machine-made and polyester flags.
The Bureau of Indian Standards specifies nine standard sizes, from 6300 × 4200 mm down to 150 × 100 mm for cars and tables.
Until a 2004 Supreme Court ruling, private citizens could fly the flag only on certain national days.
clues: Saffron, white and green horizontal stripes with a navy wheel in the middle.
Its central wheel has 24 spokes and comes from an emperor's stone pillar.
A spinning wheel was replaced by a wheel of law weeks before independence.
Its flag code once required the flag to be made from hand-spun cloth.

name: Japan
nickname: Nisshōki (sun-mark flag), commonly Hinomaru (circle of the sun)
summary: A red disc centred on a white field. The disc represents the sun, which holds a central place in Japanese tradition: the imperial house traces its descent from the sun goddess Amaterasu, and the country's name, Nippon or Nihon, means 'origin of the sun'.
origin: Sun-disc fans and banners appear in Japan from the late Heian and Kamakura periods, and the red sun on white was used by samurai clans and on trading ships during the Edo period.

In 1854 the Tokugawa shogunate ordered Japanese ships to fly the Hinomaru to distinguish them from foreign vessels. After the Meiji Restoration, Proclamation No. 57 of 1870 made it the flag for merchant ships, with a 7:10 ratio and the disc shifted one-hundredth of the length toward the hoist.

For more than a century the Hinomaru was the de facto national flag without a law to that effect. The Act on National Flag and Anthem of 13 August 1999 made it official, set the ratio at 2:3, centred the disc, and fixed its diameter at three-fifths of the flag's height. The law followed a debate over the flag's association with wartime militarism.

symbols.name: Red disc
symbols.description: A centred circle with a diameter of three-fifths of the flag's height.
symbols.meaning: The sun, linked to the imperial line's mythical descent from Amaterasu and to the country's name.

history.label: Hinomaru (7:10, disc slightly off-centre)
history.note: Set by Proclamation No. 57 for merchant ships and used as the de facto national flag.

history.label: Nisshōki (2:3, centred disc)
history.note: Made official by the Act on National Flag and Anthem.

facts: The rising-sun flag with sixteen red rays (Kyokujitsu-ki) is a separate flag, still used by the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force.
Bangladesh's flag also has a red disc, but on green and set toward the hoist.
Palau's flag uses a similar off-centre disc, in yellow on light blue, representing the moon.
clues: A single red circle centred on a white field, nothing else.
Its disc used to sit very slightly toward the hoist until a 1999 law centred it.
The disc evokes a goddess from whom an imperial dynasty claims descent.

name: Kenya
summary: Black, red and green horizontal bands separated by thin white stripes, with a red, black and white Maasai shield and two crossed white spears in the centre. It was raised at independence at midnight on 12 December 1963.
origin: The flag is based on that of the Kenya African National Union (KANU), the party that led Kenya to independence. KANU's black, red and green flag was itself derived from the colours of the Kenya African Union.

For the national flag, white fimbriations were added between the bands, and the party's emblem was replaced with a traditional Maasai shield and spears. The flag was raised as the Union Flag came down at the independence ceremony in Nairobi.

facts: The flag is protected by the National Flag, Emblems and Names Act.
Its colours echo the Pan-African red, black and green of Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association flag.
clues: Black, red and green bands with thin white stripes, and a shield and two spears in the centre.
The shield on it is of a traditional pastoralist people's design.
Its colours come from the party that led the country to independence in 1963.

name: Lebanon
summary: A white band twice the height of the red bands above and below it, bearing a green Lebanese cedar that touches both red bands. It was adopted in the weeks after Lebanon's independence from the French Mandate in 1943.
origin: The cedar of Lebanon has been a symbol of the region since antiquity and is mentioned in the Hebrew Bible dozens of times. Maronite Christians adopted it as an emblem in the 18th century, and under the French Mandate (1920–1943) Lebanon used a French tricolour with a cedar in the white band.

On 7 December 1943, shortly after the National Pact and the declaration of independence of 22 November, Parliament amended Article 5 of the Constitution to define the new flag. Members of Parliament had sketched an early version during the independence crisis in November 1943.

colors.name: Green

symbols.name: Cedar of Lebanon
symbols.description: A green cedar (Cedrus libani) centred in the white band, its width one-third of the flag's length, touching both red bands.
symbols.meaning: Holiness, eternity, steadfastness and peace; it recalls biblical verses such as Psalm 92:12, 'The righteous shall flourish… like a cedar in Lebanon'.

history.label: French Mandate flag
history.note: The French tricolour with a cedar in the white band.

facts: The constitution says the cedar should be green; some older flags showed a cedar with a brown trunk.
It is one of the few national flags with a tree as its central emblem.
clues: A green tree on a white band between two red bands.
Its central tree touches both of the coloured bands.
Before independence its tree sat on a European tricolour.

name: Mexico
designer: Coat of arms redrawn by Francisco Eppens Helguera (1968)
summary: A vertical tricolour of green, white and red with the national coat of arms in the centre: a golden eagle on a prickly pear cactus, devouring a snake. The emblem retells the Aztec legend of the founding of Tenochtitlan, today's Mexico City.
origin: The colours come from the flag of the Army of the Three Guarantees, which won independence from Spain in 1821. Its three guarantees were religion (Catholicism), independence and union between Spaniards and Mexicans.

The first national flag of 1821 placed a crowned eagle on a cactus in the white band. The design changed with each regime: republican eagles without crowns, the Habsburg crown of Maximilian's Second Empire, and Porfirio Díaz's French-styled eagle.

In 1916 Venustiano Carranza decreed a profile eagle in the style of Aztec codices. The current version, drawn by Francisco Eppens Helguera, was adopted on 16 September 1968, shortly before Mexico City hosted the Olympic Games, and confirmed by the 1984 Law on the National Arms, Flag and Anthem.

colors.name: Green
colors.meaning: Originally independence; in the secular reading promoted after the 19th-century Reform era, hope.

colors.name: White
colors.meaning: Originally the purity of the Catholic faith; later read as unity.

colors.name: Red
colors.meaning: Originally the union of Europeans and Americans; later read as the blood of national heroes.

symbols.name: Eagle devouring a snake
symbols.description: A golden eagle in profile, perched on its left talon on a prickly pear (nopal) cactus and holding a serpent in its right talon and beak.
symbols.meaning: The Aztec legend in which the god Huitzilopochtli told the Mexica to found their city where they saw an eagle on a cactus eating a serpent. They founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco around 1325.

symbols.name: Nopal cactus on a rock in the lake
symbols.description: The cactus bears red fruit and grows from a rock rising out of water, drawn in Aztec glyph style.
symbols.meaning: The site of Tenochtitlan. The name Tenochtitlan is often glossed as 'place of the prickly pear cactus on the rock'.

symbols.name: Oak and laurel branches
symbols.description: A semicircular wreath of oak and laurel tied with a ribbon in the national colours.
symbols.meaning: Strength (oak) and victory (laurel).

history.label: First Mexican Empire
history.note: Crowned eagle on a cactus.

history.label: First Republic
history.note: Uncrowned eagle with a snake, framed by branches.

history.label: Second Mexican Empire
history.note: Maximilian's flag with crowned eagles in each corner.

history.label: Restored Republic and Porfiriato
history.note: Frontal eagle in a European heraldic style.

history.label: Carranza's eagle
history.note: Profile eagle in Aztec-codex style.

history.label: Current flag
history.note: Eppens' redrawing of the arms.

facts: Mexican Flag Day is 24 February, the anniversary of the Plan of Iguala in 1821.
Italy's flag uses the same colours in the same order but with a 2:3 ratio and no emblem; Mexico's colours are also darker.
Its 4:7 ratio is unusually long.
clues: Green, white and red vertical bands with an eagle eating a snake on a cactus.
Its emblem retells the founding legend of a city built on a lake.
Remove its emblem and it closely resembles a European flag.
Its current emblem was redrawn just before its capital hosted the Olympics.

summary: Green, black and yellow horizontal bands edged in white, with a red triangle at the hoist bearing a yellow star, an open book, a hoe and an AK-47 rifle with a bayonet. It is the only national flag to show a modern assault rifle.
origin: The flag derives from that of FRELIMO, the Mozambique Liberation Front, which fought Portuguese colonial rule from 1964 until independence in 1975.

Independent Mozambique's first flags were based closely on the FRELIMO flag. The current version, with the emblem from the national coat of arms placed in the red triangle, was adopted on 1 May 1983. Its meanings are written into the Constitution.

facts: A 2005 public competition to redesign the flag, prompted partly by objections to the rifle, ended without any change.
Guatemala's coat of arms shows crossed rifles, and Haiti's shows cannons and muskets, but Mozambique's is the only national flag with a modern assault rifle.

name: Nepal
summary: Two stacked crimson pennants with a blue border, a white moon in the upper one and a white sun in the lower. It is the only non-rectangular national flag, and its constitution sets out its construction as a step-by-step geometric procedure.
origin: Triangular pennants have flown over the Indian subcontinent and Himalayas for centuries. The double pennant was in use well before the 20th century; older versions drew the sun and moon with human faces.

On 16 December 1962 a new constitution standardised the flag, removed the faces from the sun and moon and set out a detailed geometric construction. The interim constitution of 2007 and the Constitution of Nepal of 2015 keep the same flag and construction in Schedule 1.

colors.name: Crimson
colors.meaning: Nepal's national colour and the colour of the rhododendron, the national flower; also read as bravery.

colors.name: Blue
colors.meaning: Peace and harmony.

colors.name: White
colors.meaning: The sun and the moon.

symbols.name: Two pennants
symbols.description: Two overlapping right-angled triangles, the upper smaller, forming a double pennant.
symbols.meaning: Often said to stand for the Himalayas, or for Hinduism and Buddhism, the country's two main religions.

symbols.name: Moon
symbols.description: A white crescent with eight rays in the upper pennant.
symbols.meaning: The hope that Nepal will last as long as the sun and moon; also read as the calm, cool temperament of the Nepali people.

symbols.name: Sun
symbols.description: A twelve-rayed white sun in the lower pennant.
symbols.meaning: The hope for the nation's permanence; also read as fierce resolve and the heat of the lowlands.

history.label: Traditional double pennant
history.note: The sun and moon were drawn with human faces.

history.label: Standardised flag
history.note: Faces removed and geometry fixed by the 1962 constitution.

facts: Schedule 1 of the Constitution gives numbered geometric steps for drawing the flag; its proportions involve an irrational number, roughly 1:1.2190.
It is the only national flag that is not a rectangle. Ohio's swallowtail is the only non-rectangular US state flag.
Its national colour, crimson, is also the colour of the rhododendron.
clues: The only national flag that is not a rectangle.
Two stacked crimson pennants with a blue border.
A white moon above and a white sun below.
Its constitution gives step-by-step geometric instructions for drawing it.

name: South Africa
summary: A horizontal Y (a 'pall') in green, edged in white and gold, splitting a red upper band and a blue lower band, with a black triangle at the hoist. With six colours and no emblem, it was designed in weeks for the country's first democratic election.
origin: South Africa's previous flag, the 'Oranje-Blanje-Blou' of 1928, was based on the Dutch Prinsenvlag and carried miniature flags of the United Kingdom, the Orange Free State and the South African Republic. It was closely tied to apartheid.

In 1993 the Transitional Executive Council held a public competition that drew more than 7,000 entries, none of them accepted. With the April 1994 election weeks away, State Herald Frederick Brownell produced the final design, which was approved on 15 March 1994 as an interim flag.
It was first raised on 27 April 1994, the day of the election, and was confirmed as the national flag in the 1996 Constitution.

facts: It was one of the few national flags with six colours and no seal or emblem when adopted.
Officially the design has no symbolism; the government suggests people read it as convergence and unity.
It was designed only weeks before it was first flown.
clues: A green horizontal Y separates red and blue bands, with a black triangle at the hoist.
Six colours, no emblem, designed by a state herald in a matter of weeks.
First raised on the day of its country's first fully democratic election.
It replaced an orange-white-blue flag carrying three miniature flags.

name: United Kingdom
summary: Three national crosses layered into one: the red cross of St George for England, the white saltire of St Andrew for Scotland, and the red saltire of St Patrick for Ireland. Wales is not represented, because it was already united with England when the first Union Flag was made.
origin: When James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, the two crowns were joined in one person. A royal proclamation of 12 April 1606 created a flag for ships of both kingdoms combining the cross of St George and the saltire of St Andrew.

That first Union Flag remained in use (with a break under Cromwell) until the Act of Union with Ireland took effect on 1 January 1801. The saltire of St Patrick was then added, counterchanged with St Andrew's saltire so that neither Scotland nor Ireland took precedence: the red saltire is offset, so the white is broader above it on the hoist side.

Because of this offset the flag has a right way up. In the upper hoist quarter the broad white band sits above the red diagonal; flying it the other way is regarded as a distress signal or simple error.

facts: The name 'Union Jack' probably comes from the jack, a small flag flown at the bow of a ship. Both 'Union Flag' and 'Union Jack' are accepted names.
The Union Flag appears in the canton of the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and Tuvalu, and in many British overseas territories and Canadian provinces.
On land it is often made in 3:5 proportions; the 1:2 form is used at sea and by the government.
clues: Three national crosses, one upright and two diagonal, overlaid on a blue field.
It has a correct way up because its diagonal crosses are offset.
One constituent country is not represented on it at all.
It sits in the canton of several other national flags in Oceania.

nickname: The Stars and Stripes, Old Glory, the Star-Spangled Banner
designer: 50-star arrangement attributed to Robert G. Heft (1958)
summary: Thirteen horizontal stripes of red and white with a blue canton of fifty white stars. The stripes stand for the thirteen original colonies and the stars for the states; the canton has changed 26 times as states joined the Union.
origin: The first widely flown flag of the rebelling colonies was the Grand Union (or Continental Colours) flag of 1775–1777: thirteen red and white stripes with the British Union Flag in the canton.

On 14 June 1777 the Second Continental Congress passed the first Flag Resolution: the flag would be thirteen stripes, alternate red and white, with thirteen white stars on a blue field "representing a new constellation". The resolution gave no arrangement for the stars, so early flags varied widely. The story that Betsy Ross sewed the first flag comes from her grandson in 1870 and is not supported by contemporary evidence; Francis Hopkinson, a signer of the Declaration of Independence, claimed credit for the design.

The Flag Act of 1794 added two stars and two stripes for Vermont and Kentucky; this 15-stripe flag flew over Fort McHenry in 1814 and inspired Francis Scott Key's 'The Star-Spangled Banner'. The Flag Act of 1818 returned to thirteen stripes for good and set the rule still in force: one star per state, added on the Fourth of July after a state's admission.

The current 50-star flag became official on 4 July 1960, after Hawaii's admission. Its arrangement of nine offset rows of six and five stars is credited to Robert G. Heft, who designed it as a high-school project in Ohio.

history.label: 50 stars

facts: The 50-star flag has been in use longer than any previous version.
Flag Day, 14 June, marks the 1777 Flag Resolution.
The colour meanings come from Charles Thomson's 1782 description of the Great Seal, which uses the same colours; Congress never assigned meanings to the flag itself.
The US Flag Code governs etiquette but carries no penalties; the Supreme Court ruled in Texas v. Johnson (1989) that flag burning is protected speech.
clues: Thirteen horizontal stripes of red and white and a blue canton full of white stars.
Its canton has been redesigned more than twenty times, a new version each time the federation grew.
A star is added on the Fourth of July after a new member joins.
A version with fifteen stripes inspired a national anthem written during a bombardment in 1814.
